bearings.paper_claim: Fairshake raised a record $203 million for the 2024 cycle, reported as more than MAGA Inc. and Senate Majority PAC. These are receipts. The paper also reports $78 million raised toward the 2026 midterms 'to date' as of its January 2025 date. The text gives no FEC source for either figure and cites press items.
bearings.paper_location: p. 7 ($203M and the MAGA Inc. and Senate Majority PAC comparison); p. 9 ($78M to date); p. 13 (more money than any other super PAC in the 2024 cycle)
bearings.system_side: Refit registry declines crypto for the pac, control and lobbying models. Reason given: no growth series and no OpenSecrets code today. Verified: all three model flags are false and the reason text matches.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The figures show a large money series appearing for 2024 and early 2026. They do not establish a level break, a first cycle, or any per-cycle history before 2024, so they cannot by themselves justify a break term. Any admission would still need FEC-sourced totals.
bearings.verifier_note: Numbers and the registry decline check out. The analyst's claim that a new entrant spent at record scale in its first big cycle is not in the paper, which says only that Fairshake is the largest pro-crypto super PAC. Receipts-versus-spending wording corrected. Attaching refs 28, 30 and 34 to specific figures is the analyst's mapping, not the paper's.

bearings.paper_claim: Fairshake, Protect Progress and Defend American Jobs ran ads that often did not mention cryptocurrency, focusing on candidate integrity or economic policy. Named races: Fairshake backed Moreno against Brown in Ohio and opposed Tester in Montana. The paper also cites opposition to Porter in a California Senate primary and to Bowman's re-election bid. Coinbase, Ripple and Andreessen Horowitz each gave tens of millions of dollars, with no exact figures. No oppose or support split of dollars is given.
bearings.paper_location: pp. 7-10 (Ohio and Montana pp. 7-8; ads p. 8; donors p. 8; Porter and Bowman pp. 9-10)
bearings.system_side: Crypto workbook builder has a Super PAC scope and a Corporate tier (scopes list near lines 550-583) and a support_oppose field on rows (near line 177). The transfer graph reads only 24G and 24K outgoing OTH records and never counts independent expenditures again as transfers (docstring, lines 1-7). Code side verified.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Qualitative evidence for federal races in 2024 only. It supports keeping support and oppose separate rather than netting them, and supports the point that ad topic cannot be read from ad content. It does not support any oppose share, and the paper's own examples include backing candidates as well as opposing them.
bearings.verifier_note: Code references check out. The paper does not say crypto spending ran through super PACs in general, nor that it is corporate-treasury, independent-expenditure or oppose-heavy; the analyst added those. The 89 percent figure is not crypto-specific: the brain R12 audit (mentat-fec-pipeline-history-audit-r12) reports oppose at 89.0 percent of an all-industry $2.77 billion beneficiary total and calls the Beneficiary Summary 89 percent inverted. It is not a crypto workbook figure.

bearings.paper_claim: The paper reports that Fairshake raised $203 million (receipts, p. 7). It does not say how that money was spent, does not split it into independent expenditures versus PAC contributions to candidate committees, and gives no crypto dollar figure for either channel. The bearing's claim that most of it was independent expenditure is not in the paper.
bearings.system_side: flip_model ind0 equals banks plus finserv PAC fields from congestion.json, measured against member receipts R. money_observation.industry_money_missing imputes only when no money observation exists. Code lines verified as written. The claim that IEs and crypto money are absent rests on those field definitions, which were not traced to their source.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The structural point, that a super PAC outside-spending channel is outside the ind0 term, is a code observation this paper can only illustrate. The paper gives no effect size and no CU-specific case, so it cannot size the b term or justify an IE weight.
bearings.verifier_note: The paper does not say that most crypto electoral money was independent expenditure rather than candidate-committee contributions; it reports receipts only, so the original paper claim is refuted. The code-side observation stands on its own and is not established by this paper. The rewritten fields state only what the paper supports.

bearings.paper_claim: Fairshake campaigned against Katie Porter in California's Senate primary and opposed Jamaal Bowman's re-election bid. The paper calls this influence 'decisive' and offers no counterfactual or estimate.
bearings.system_side: build_electoral_plays.py lines 30-34: for a genuine Opponent the primary route scores the same-party improvement gap and the general route scores the cross-party flip gap, and the value is the larger of the two. Verified.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Shows that federal primary-contest plays by an industry actor occurred in 2024. It is not evidence that such plays work, because outcomes are confounded and there is no comparison group. Do not use it to calibrate conversion.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper claim verified (Porter and Bowman on pp. 9-10; decisive wording there). The system side said contest plays convert opponents in spread(); build_electoral_plays.py contains no spread(). A spread() exists in fec/engine/budget_frontier.py (line 118), but it was not checked as the conversion step, so that reference is removed here.

related.why: Estimates effects of post-Citizens United independent-group TV ads on Senate and governor vote shares and turnout, with a confounding adjustment. It is the kind of causal evidence the paper's decisive-influence claims lack. Item summary checked.
Finds low overlap between organizational lobbying and PAC giving across 1998-2018, which fits crypto's electoral channel running apart from LDA activity. Item summary checked.

Estimates CFscores from contribution records and tests whether donors give for ideology or for investor and partisan-electoral motives. That is a test framework for the targeting Chohan describes but does not test. Item summary checked; the link to Fairshake targeting is interpretive.
Paul's cross-industry report covers Crypto among five financial-services industries, so Chohan supplies narrative context for that sector. Item summary checked.

Randomized field experiment finding that contributions facilitate access to House offices, not electoral outcomes. It is adjacent to Chohan's unestimated influence claim rather than a direct contradiction, so the relation was changed from contradicts.

summary_issues: rel.summary_md calls crypto money corporate-treasury, mostly independent expenditure and often spent against candidates, and says it is oppose-heavy. The paper says none of this; it gives receipts, a few named races, and no oppose share.
rel.summary_md and bearing 1 say a new entrant spent at record scale in its first big cycle. The paper does not say Fairshake is new or that 2024 was its first big cycle.

rel.summary_md says the brain records 89 percent of beneficiary dollars as oppose for crypto. The 89.0 percent figure is the all-industry R12 audit total of $2.77 billion, not a crypto figure, and the same note calls that summary 89 percent inverted.
Bearing 3 paper_claim (most crypto electoral money was independent expenditure, not candidate contributions) is not in the paper, which reports receipts only. Refuted and rewritten.
Bearing 4 system_side says contest plays convert opponents in spread(); build_electoral_plays.py has no spread(). Removed.
Related link anon-2025-cross-industry-political was dropped: its stated same-data relation is false. The memo covers life insurance, mutual funds, credit unions and commercial banking, not crypto.
Related link kalla-nd-campaign-contributions-facilitate changed from contradicts to complements, because the study measures access to offices, not electoral outcomes.
Related link bonica-2013 description overstated the framework as applied to Fairshake targeting; the reason was narrowed.
Short quote in ext (p. 14) is not verbatim. The paper reads 'What we now witness is a crypto-oligarchy that mirrors the broader historical evolution'; the quoted fragment drops 'that'.

paul_alignment quotes Paul's Kim J. 2025 margin note as 'presence'. The annotation digest (_work/pdf_annotations_digest.md, line 1994) reads 'pressance'. The Kim note itself was not opened, so the wording was not confirmed from the source PDF.
Specific figures are attached to reference numbers (refs 28, 30, 34) that the text never cites at those numbers. These attachments are the analyst's inference, not the paper's sourcing.

Coverage limits: the Mentat attributed-estimate producer claim and the Melange congestion.json field definitions were not traced; the SSRN number in the metadata hint is absent from the text, as ext notes.
